issues.text: In a US review of 120 older veterans given a loop diuretic after swelling from gabapentin or pregabalin, about 1 in 4 had a possible diuretic-related problem within 2 months: worse kidney function, a drop in blood pressure on standing, abnormal salts or a fall. Small study, no comparison group.
issues.problem: States as fact that the swelling in these veterans came from gabapentin or pregabalin. The study only identified people who started a loop diuretic after starting a gabapentinoid (a 'potential' cascade) and found clinicians recorded the gabapentinoid as a possible cause in only 4 of 120. It is also a study of a different first drug, not of calcium channel blockers, and the group was 97% male. The evidence record's safe wording ('after a nerve-pain medicine caused swelling') overstates the abstract.
issues.source_says: Growdon 2025 abstract: 120 US veterans aged 66+ who 'potentially experienced the gabapentinoid-LD prescribing cascade'; 'Gabapentinoids were rarely noted in the differential (n = 4 [3.3%])'; 28 patients (23.3%) had 37 events 'potentially attributable to LD initiation' in 60 days; 116 of 120 male; no comparison group.
issues.replacement: In a US record review of 120 older veterans, mostly men, who were started on a loop diuretic after starting gabapentin or pregabalin, about 1 in 4 had an event within 2 months that may have been due to the diuretic: worse kidney function, a drop in blood pressure on standing, abnormal salts or a fall. Small study, no comparison group, and not a study of calcium channel blockers.

issues.text: A prescribing cascade is when a side effect of one medicine is taken for a new illness, and a second medicine is started to treat it.
issues.problem: Definition drops the key element: the side effect is misread as a new illness. 'Taken for' also fits a deliberate, appropriate second drug, which the evidence record notes exist.
issues.source_says: Savage 2020: 'A prescribing cascade occurs when the edema is misinterpreted as a new medical condition and a diuretic is subsequently prescribed to treat the edema.' McCarthy 2022: 'typically when a side effect is misinterpreted as a new condition.'
issues.replacement: A prescribing cascade is when a side effect of one medicine is mistaken for a new illness, and a second medicine is started to treat it.

issues.text: In a UK study, 120 people taking a statin read that constipation was a 'common' side effect. On average they guessed 34 in 100 people would get it. The figure used in the study was 2.5 in 100.
issues.problem: Wrong denominator. The 120 people were split across two side effects (constipation or pancreatitis) and across word or number versions; only the constipation-with-word group (a fraction of the 120) read 'common' and gave the 34 in 100 average. Writing '120 people ... read that constipation was common' makes a subgroup look like the whole study.
issues.source_says: Knapp 2004: 120 adults on simvastatin or atorvastatin; each given a written statement about one side effect (constipation or pancreatitis); within each side effect half got words and half numbers; constipation mean estimate 34.2% (words) vs 8.1% (number 2.5%).
issues.replacement: In a UK study of 120 people taking a statin, those told that constipation was a 'common' side effect guessed on average that 34 in 100 people would get it. The figure used in the study was 2.5 in 100.

issues.text: In a study in Leeds, 120 people taking a statin read that constipation was a 'common' side effect. On average they guessed that 34 in 100 people would get it. The figure used in the study was 2.5 in 100. People given that number guessed about 8 in 100: still too high, but far closer.
issues.problem: Same denominator error as X: the 34 in 100 and 8 in 100 averages come from the constipation groups only, not from all 120.
issues.source_says: Knapp 2004 abstract: 'Within each side effect condition half the patients were given the information in verbal form and half in numerical form'.
issues.replacement: In a study in Leeds, 120 people taking a statin were each given a written statement about one side effect. Those told that constipation was 'common' guessed on average that 34 in 100 people would get it. The figure used in the study was 2.5 in 100. Those told the number guessed about 8 in 100: still too high, but far closer.

issues.text: Several called it a 'tick box' exercise.

The same interviewees distinguished simple reviews (younger patients, few medicines), which could be done quickly without the patient, from complex reviews (frail older people on many medicines), which they said should get more patient-centred appointments. For a post aimed at older people, omitting that makes the finding sound more uniform than reported (though the authors also say time pressure limited involvement even for complex patients).

issues.text: In a small volunteer study, a heating pad raised fentanyl blood levels to almost 3 times higher while it was on.
issues.problem: The 'almost 3 times' is the peak and total exposure in the first 4 hours after a new patch went on with heat versus without (10 volunteers). Over the whole 36 hours there was no significant difference. 'While it was on' leaves out that timing.
issues.source_says: Ashburn 2003 abstract: 'During a period of 36 hours, there were no significant differences in C(max), AUC, or T(max) ... issues.replacement: In a small volunteer study (10 people), heating a new fentanyl patch for its first 4 hours gave blood levels almost 3 times higher over those hours.

issues.text: OPERAM: 2,008 people aged 70 or over in hospital, each on 5 or more regular medicines. A doctor and a pharmacist reviewed them with STOPP/START software.
issues.problem: False as written. Only the intervention wards (963 of 2,008; 916 actually received the review) were reviewed. The rest had usual care, and the later comparison with them is the whole point of the post.

issues.replacement: OPERAM: 2,008 people aged 70 or over in hospital, each on 5 or more regular medicines, were assigned by ward to a medicines review or usual care. In the review group, a doctor and a pharmacist used STOPP/START software.

issues.text:
OPERAM reviewed the medicines of 2,008 people aged 70+ in hospital and flagged a problem for 86 in 100.

issues.source_says: Cole 2023 (Cochrane): 38 studies; 'It is uncertain whether pharmaceutical care reduces the proportion of patients with one or more PIM ... very low-certainty evidence'; hospital admissions and quality of life 'little or no difference' (low certainty).
issues.replacement: A Cochrane review of 38 trials of medicines reviews and similar pharmaceutical care found it uncertain whether they reduce inappropriate prescribing, with low or very low certainty evidence.

issues.text:
Doctors discharging older people were asked one question: will this person be harmed by their medicines in the next 8 weeks?

Their predictions showed no clear link with who was.
issues.problem: The outcome is mis-stated. Doctors predicted medication-related harm that required healthcare (readmission or community healthcare), not any harm. The 37 in 100 with 'some harm' is a wider outcome than the one predicted, and the prediction analysis covered 1,066 patients, not 1,116.
issues.source_says: Parekh 2018 (prediction) abstract: doctors 'predicted the likelihood of their patient experiencing MRH requiring healthcare (hospital readmission or community healthcare) in the initial 8-week period'; 1066 patients analysed; OR 1.10 (0.82 to 1.46). The record's own safe wording drops 'requiring healthcare'.
issues.replacement:
Doctors discharging older people were asked to predict whether this person would have a medicines problem needing healthcare (a hospital readmission or community healthcare) in the next 8 weeks.

Their predictions showed no clear link with who did.

issues.text: We think older people going home on changed medicines should get routine medicines follow-up. That is a judgement.
issues.problem: A service-policy position (routine follow-up for a whole group) that neither paper tests; the post itself says benefit of follow-up is not settled. It is also stronger than the X version, which says only that follow-up should not depend on a hunch.
issues.source_says: Parekh 2018 (incidence) Discussion: 'it remains unclear from randomized trials if medication review on its own reduces MRH'; prediction paper concludes only that doctors' judgement 'is not a reliable tool to predict MRH'.
issues.replacement: We think who gets medicines follow-up after discharge should not depend on a hunch. That is a judgement.

issues.text: Then the prediction study. Most predictions came from doctors in their first few years after qualifying, who usually write the discharge.

issues.replacement: Three quarters of the harm events came from medicines prescribed at discharge.

issues.text: Many hospitals now have pharmacists checking lists, which helps but does not remove every gap.

issues.replacement: This review is older (studies up to 2005) and covered prescription medicines only, so current rates may differ.

issues.text: In one English survey, about 1 in 3 older people on prescribed medicines also took a supplement or herbal remedy. Some combinations can interact; the one most often reported is a raised bleeding risk with ginkgo, garlic or ginseng taken with aspirin or warfarin.
issues.problem: Two sources are run together. The survey (two English practices, 155 of 400 replied, 38.8%) found 1 in 3 using supplements and 'potential' interactions; the ginkgo, garlic, ginseng with aspirin or warfarin finding comes from a separate systematic review. Low response rate is not mentioned, and the interactions are potential, not observed harm.
issues.source_says: Agbabiaka 2018: 155 returned (response rate 38.8%), concurrent use 33.6%, 'Sixteen participants (32.6%) were at risk of potential adverse drug interactions'. Agbabiaka 2017 review: 'Potential risks of bleeding due to the use of Ginkgo biloba, garlic or ginseng with aspirin or warfarin was the most reported herb-drug interaction.'
issues.replacement: In one small English survey (155 replies, 39% response), about 1 in 3 older people on prescribed medicines also took a supplement or herbal remedy. Some combinations could interact; in a review of studies, the one most often reported was a possible raised bleeding risk with ginkgo, garlic or ginseng taken with aspirin or warfarin.

issues.text: In US national data from 2001 to 2010, more than half of older people in poor health had an HbA1c below 7% (53 mmol/mol), about as often as healthy older people, and just over half of those were on insulin or a sulfonylurea.
issues.problem: Two errors. (1) The population is older people with diabetes; as written it says more than half of all older people in poor health had an HbA1c below 7%, which is meaningless or false. (2) 'Just over half of those' swaps a whole-sample figure (54.9% of everyone with HbA1c below 7%) for the poor-health group, where it was 60.0%.
issues.source_says: Lipska 2015 abstract: 1,288 US adults 65+ with diabetes, NHANES 2001-2010; HbA1c below 7% in 56.4% of the very complex/poor health group (62.8% relatively healthy); of those with HbA1c below 7%, 54.9% overall and 60.0% in the very complex/poor health group were on insulin or a sulfonylurea. Poor health defined as difficulty with 2+ activities of daily living or dialysis.
issues.replacement: In US national data from 2001 to 2010, 56 in 100 older people with diabetes who were in very poor health (needing help with two or more everyday activities, or on dialysis) had an HbA1c below 7% (53 mmol/mol), about as often as healthy older people with diabetes (63 in 100). Of those in very poor health with an HbA1c below 7%, 6 in 10 were on insulin or a sulfonylurea.

issues.text: In a small US study of 40 older people on insulin whose HbA1c was high, 26 had low readings over 3 days of continuous monitoring, and 93 in 100 of those episodes were missed by finger-prick tests and symptoms.
issues.problem: Not all 40 were on insulin (37 were), 'high' is 8% or more (mean 9.3%), and 'low readings' means glucose below 70 mg/dL. The 93 in 100 is of 102 episodes.
issues.source_says: Munshi 2011: 40 adults aged 69+, HbA1c 8% or higher, 37 (93%) on insulin; 26 (65%) had at least one glucose below 70 mg/dL; 95 of 102 episodes (93%) unrecognised.
issues.replacement: In a small US study of 40 older people (37 on insulin) whose HbA1c was 8% or more, 26 had low glucose readings (below 70 mg/dL) over 3 days of continuous monitoring, and 93 in 100 of the 102 low episodes were missed by finger-prick tests and symptoms.

issues.text: A 2026 review recommends that hospitals let people take their own medicines where it is safe.

issues.source_says: Delf and Wright 2026 abstract: 'Four studies met the inclusion criteria ... Findings suggest the need to strengthen systems supporting timely medication administration, enable self-administration where appropriate'.

issues.replacement: In a US hospital system, a levodopa dose was missed on about 1 hospital day in 5 (days where the home timing was known).

issues.text: Two UK studies link anti-inflammatory painkillers taken with these medicines to sudden kidney injury. The risk was highest with all three together. One study found it greatest in the first month; the other, in people over 75 and in people with weaker kidneys.
issues.problem: The two studies disagree on the two-drug combinations, and the post hides it. The English GP-records study found no extra risk with an anti-inflammatory plus only a water tablet or only an ACE inhibitor/ARB; the Scottish study did, with a similar relative increase and a smaller absolute one. 'Highest with all three' is true only for absolute risk; in the Scottish study the relative increase was about the same (rate ratio 1.64 against 1.60 and 1.64).
issues.source_says: Lapi 2013 abstract: 'current use of a double therapy combination ... with NSAIDs was not associated with an increased rate of acute kidney injury', triple RR 1.31. Dreischulte 2015 abstract: relative increase 'similar' in triple (1.64) and dual (1.60, 1.64) combinations; 'numbers needed to harm ... 158 vs. over 300'.
issues.replacement: Two UK studies looked at this. Both link an anti-inflammatory painkiller taken with a water tablet and an ACE inhibitor or ARB to sudden kidney injury. Only the Scottish one also found extra risk with just one of the two; there, the extra risk in absolute terms was larger with all three together. One study found it greatest in the first month; the other, in people over 75 and in people with weaker kidneys.

issues.text: The extra risk was greatest in the first month.
issues.problem: The English study's null result for the two-drug combinations is not given, and the first-month finding is left without the fact that the association was gone after 90 days. Readers of item 1 then meet 'with only one of the two' in item 2 and may take it as agreeing with item 1.
issues.source_says: Lapi 2013: first 30 days RR 1.82 (1.35 to 2.46); after more than 90 days RR 1.01 (0.84 to 1.23); double combinations 'not associated with an increased rate'.
issues.replacement: The extra risk was greatest in the first month and had gone by 90 days of use. This study found no extra risk with only one of the two blood pressure medicines.

issues.text: Linked with sudden kidney injury, most with all three together
issues.problem: 'Most' is true for absolute risk only; relative increases were similar in the Scottish study, and the English study found nothing for the two-drug combinations.
issues.source_says: Dreischulte 2015 and Lapi 2013, as above.
issues.replacement: Linked with sudden kidney injury; larger absolute risk with all three together

issues.replacement: Two UK studies link that mix with sudden kidney injury; only the Scottish one also found a risk with two, and it found the absolute extra risk larger with all three. In the Scottish one, about 1 extra kidney injury per 158 people taking an anti-inflammatory for a year alongside both medicines, not for a few days.

issues.source_says: Mc Gillicuddy 2016: 'Five studies met the inclusion criteria ... approximately 14 % ... However, evidence to support such contentions is limited.'
issues.replacement: About 1 in 7 older people living at home say they have difficulty swallowing their medicines, according to a small review of five studies.

issues.text: About 1 in 7 older people at home say they have difficulty swallowing their medicines.
issues.problem: Same omission.
issues.source_says: As above.
issues.replacement: About 1 in 7 older people at home report trouble swallowing pills (small review).

issues.text: About 1 in 7 older people at home find their tablets hard to swallow.
issues.problem: Same omission.
issues.source_says: As above.
issues.replacement: About 1 in 7 older people at home say their tablets are hard to swallow (small review).

issues.text: 1. Ask how the tablets go down. About 1 in 7 older people at home find it hard.
issues.problem: Same omission.
issues.source_says: As above.
issues.replacement: 1. Ask how the tablets go down. About 1 in 7 older people at home say they find it hard (small review).

issues.text: Older people and carers interviewed in Ireland described coping without telling anyone.
issues.problem: Overstates: the study says people coped within the regimen with a lack of focused communication with health professionals, not that they told no one.
issues.source_says: Mc Gillicuddy 2019 (record passage, abstract): people 'tend to feel resigned to coping within the constraints of the current medication regimen, resulting in a lack of focused communication with healthcare professionals'.
issues.replacement: Older people and carers interviewed in Ireland described coping without raising the problem with health professionals.

issues.text: Doses given in a way that departed from national guidance were seen at 57 in 100 observed doses for residents with swallowing difficulty, against about 31 in 100 for other residents. That counts departures from guidance, not harm.
issues.problem: Sits under the crushing list and could be read as crushing errors. The measure is any deviation from national guidance during observed drug rounds (738 administrations, 38 of 166 residents with dysphagia).
issues.source_says: Serrano Santos 2016: 'MAE rates were 57.3% and 30.8% for PWD and those without'; deviations from national guidelines classed as medication administration errors; care homes with nursing, North Yorkshire.
issues.replacement: Doses given in a way that departed from national guidance for any reason, not only crushing, were seen at 57 in 100 observed doses for residents with swallowing difficulty, against about 31 in 100 for other residents. That counts departures from guidance, not harm.

issues.text: Hiding medicine in food without the person knowing needs a formal capacity and best interests decision.
issues.problem: 'Best interests' is the England and Wales legal frame; Scotland uses different law and the sources cited do not set out the law.
issues.source_says: Majkic 2025: UK mental health trust pilot audit of covert administration (95% had a completed capacity assessment and best interests meeting); Cleary 2026 gives the definition only.
issues.replacement: Hiding medicine in food without the person knowing needs a formal decision about their capacity and care (the legal route differs across the UK).

issues.text: it needs a formal decision about the person's capacity and best interests, plus the same pharmacist check.
issues.problem: Same England and Wales framing.
issues.source_says: As above.
issues.replacement: it needs a formal decision about the person's capacity and what is best for them (the legal route differs across the UK), plus the same pharmacist check.

issues.text: Crushing an acid-coated tablet can stop it working.
issues.problem: Wrong way round and unclear: the coating protects the tablet from stomach acid (gastro-resistant); the tablet is not 'acid-coated'.
issues.source_says: Prescrire 2014: 'When a gastro-resistant layer is destroyed by crushing, underdosing is likely.'
issues.replacement: Crushing a tablet coated against stomach acid can stop it working.
